description: ByteByteGo case study documents covering real-world system design implementations

documents.title: Disney Hotstar: Scaling to 25 Million Concurrent Users

sections.title: The Challenge: Cricket Streaming at Scale
sections.content: Disney Hotstar faced an unprecedented challenge during the Indian Premier League (IPL) cricket matches, where they needed to handle 25.3 million concurrent viewers on a single stream. This represented one of the largest live streaming events globally. The challenge wasn't just raw bandwidth—it was maintaining sub-second latency while ensuring consistent quality across diverse network conditions in India, from fiber connections in metros to 3G networks in rural areas. Traditional CDN architectures would crumble under this load, requiring innovative approaches to content delivery, adaptive bitrate streaming, and edge caching strategies.

sections.title: Multi-CDN Architecture with Intelligent Routing
sections.content: Hotstar implemented a sophisticated multi-CDN strategy using AWS CloudFront, Akamai, and Cloudflare simultaneously. Their intelligent routing layer, built on top of AWS Route 53 with custom health checks, dynamically routes users to the optimal CDN based on real-time performance metrics. The system measures actual playback performance from client devices, tracking metrics like startup time, buffering ratio, and throughput. When a CDN node degrades, the routing layer automatically shifts traffic within seconds. This approach provides redundancy and maximizes available capacity across multiple providers. The video segments are pre-positioned across all CDN edges using a predictive algorithm that analyzes historical viewership patterns and pre-warms caches before major events.

sections.title: HLS with Custom Chunking Strategy
sections.content: Hotstar uses HTTP Live Streaming (HLS) with customized segment durations optimized for cricket viewing patterns. Rather than standard 6-10 second segments, they use 2-second segments for live content to minimize latency while maintaining efficient caching. Each segment is encoded at multiple quality levels (from 240p to 1080p at 60fps) using H.265 codec for better compression. The adaptive bitrate algorithm runs client-side in the player, making quality decisions every 4 segments based on measured throughput, buffer health, and device capabilities. During high-action moments in cricket (like boundaries or wickets), the system dynamically adjusts buffer targets to prevent interruptions during peak engagement periods when users are least tolerant of buffering.

sections.title: Real-Time Monitoring and Incident Response
sections.content: The platform processes over 10 billion real-time events per day from client players, ingesting metrics into a custom time-series database built on Apache Druid. Engineers monitor dozens of dashboards showing per-CDN performance, geographic patterns, device-specific issues, and business metrics like concurrent viewers and watch time. Automated alerts trigger when error rates exceed 0.1% or when buffering ratio crosses 1% for any significant cohort. The incident response team uses a custom traffic shaping tool that can gradually shift load between CDNs or reduce bitrate caps for specific regions to prevent cascading failures. This instrumentation proved critical during the record-breaking 25.3 million concurrent viewer stream, where the team made 15 real-time optimizations to maintain service quality.

sections.title: Intelligent Dasher-Order Matching
sections.content: DoorDash's matching engine processes over 1 million delivery assignments per day, making decisions in under 200 milliseconds. The system considers multiple factors: dasher location and velocity, predicted restaurant preparation time, historical dasher performance, customer delivery preferences, and dynamic demand patterns. The matching algorithm runs a constrained optimization problem balancing multiple objectives: minimizing total delivery time, maximizing dasher earnings, maintaining customer satisfaction, and ensuring fair order distribution. The engine uses machine learning models to predict preparation times with 85% accuracy within a 5-minute window, allowing it to dispatch dashers optimally so they arrive just as food is ready, minimizing wait time while keeping food hot.

sections.title: Multi-Order Batching Strategy
sections.content: To improve dasher efficiency and reduce delivery costs, DoorDash implements intelligent order batching where one dasher handles multiple orders in a single trip. The batching algorithm evaluates combinatorial possibilities in real-time, considering factors like restaurant proximity, delivery address locations, food preparation timing, and customer patience thresholds. The system uses a 30-second decision window during which it accumulates potential orders and runs an optimization that maximizes orders per delivery while keeping individual order delay under 5 minutes. The algorithm accounts for order priority (DashPass subscribers get preference), food type (ice cream orders aren't batched), and predicted traffic conditions. Batching has increased dasher earnings by 25% while maintaining customer satisfaction scores, proving that optimized logistics benefits all stakeholders.

sections.title: Machine Learning ETA Prediction
sections.content: DoorDash's ETA prediction system combines multiple ML models to provide accurate delivery time estimates. The system uses gradient boosted decision trees (XGBoost) trained on historical delivery data, considering features like restaurant busyness, dasher experience level, traffic patterns, weather conditions, and order complexity. The model is retrained nightly on the previous week's data and deployed through feature flags allowing gradual rollout. Real-time adjustments use a lightweight online learning component that corrects predictions based on live dasher location updates and GPS data. The system achieves 80% accuracy in predicting delivery times within a 5-minute window. These predictions feed both customer-facing ETAs and internal systems that trigger proactive support interventions when delays are detected.

sections.title: Geospatial Infrastructure at Scale
sections.content: The logistics platform relies on a sophisticated geospatial infrastructure built on PostgreSQL with PostGIS extensions, handling billions of location updates daily. DoorDash partitions geospatial data by metropolitan area using PostgreSQL table partitioning, with separate indexes for each city. Dasher location updates (streamed every 5 seconds) are written to Kafka topics partitioned by geographic region, then consumed by location services that update a Redis cache layer with TTL of 30 seconds. For matching queries like 'find available dashers within 2 miles of restaurant X', the system uses PostGIS's ST_DWithin function with spatial indexes (GIST indexes) that enable sub-100ms queries even with millions of active dashers. The team chose PostgreSQL over specialized geospatial databases because it simplified their architecture by consolidating their data platform, and PostGIS performance proved sufficient for their scale.

sections.title: From Monolith to Microservices
sections.content: Netflix's transition from a monolithic Java application to microservices architecture began in 2008 after a major database corruption incident that took down DVD shipping for three days. This outage catalyzed their decision to move to AWS and decompose their monolith into hundreds of specialized services. The migration took seven years (2008-2015), during which they simultaneously ran the monolith and gradually extracted functionality into services. They started with stateless services like recommendation and search, then tackled stateful services like user profiles and viewing history. The decomposition followed domain-driven design principles, creating bounded contexts around business capabilities like content catalog, billing, streaming, and recommendation. By 2025, Netflix operates over 1000 microservices handling 200+ million subscribers globally, processing billions of requests daily with 99.99% availability.

sections.title: Zuul API Gateway and Edge Services
sections.content: Netflix built Zuul, an edge service framework that acts as the front door for all Netflix client requests. Zuul provides dynamic routing, monitoring, resiliency, security, and insights into production traffic. The gateway handles device-specific API composition—mobile apps receive optimized payloads while smart TVs get different data structures. Zuul implements intelligent request routing with fallback capabilities; if a service is degraded, it can route to backup instances or return cached responses. The gateway also enforces rate limiting, authentication, and request/response transformations. Netflix processes over 2 billion requests per day through Zuul, with each request passing through multiple filters for logging, authentication, routing, and decoration. The system uses non-blocking I/O with Netty under the hood, enabling high throughput with minimal resource consumption.

sections.title: Hystrix Circuit Breaker Pattern
sections.content: Netflix created Hystrix (now in maintenance mode, succeeded by Resilience4j) to implement the circuit breaker pattern across their microservices architecture. When services make calls to dependencies, Hystrix wraps each call in a command object that monitors for failures. If failure rate exceeds a threshold (default 50% over 20 requests in 10 seconds), the circuit 'opens' and subsequent calls immediately return fallback responses without attempting the network call. After a sleep window (default 5 seconds), the circuit enters 'half-open' state, allowing one test request through. If successful, the circuit closes; if failed, it reopens. This prevents cascading failures where slow or failing services exhaust thread pools and bring down dependent services. Hystrix also provides request collapsing to batch multiple concurrent requests into a single backend call, and bulkheads to isolate thread pools per dependency, preventing one failing service from consuming all threads.

sections.title: Chaos Engineering with Chaos Monkey
sections.content: Netflix pioneered chaos engineering, deliberately injecting failures into production systems to build confidence in system resilience. Chaos Monkey randomly terminates EC2 instances during business hours, forcing engineers to design services that gracefully handle instance failures. The Simian Army expanded this concept with additional tools: Latency Monkey introduces artificial delays, Chaos Gorilla simulates entire AWS availability zone failures, and Chaos Kong tests region-wide outages. These tools run continuously in production, creating a Darwinian environment where only resilient architectures survive. Netflix's chaos engineering philosophy assumes failures are inevitable—networks are unreliable, services will be slow, instances will crash. By proactively causing failures, they surface weaknesses before they cause customer-facing outages. This approach requires strong observability, automated recovery mechanisms, and a culture that views failures as learning opportunities rather than incidents to avoid.

documents.title: Spotify: Event-Driven Architecture for Music Streaming

sections.title: Google Cloud Pub/Sub for Event Delivery
sections.content: Spotify's backend architecture centers on event-driven patterns using Google Cloud Pub/Sub as their primary message broker. The platform processes over 10 million events per second, including playback events, user interactions, playlist modifications, and social features. Each domain publishes events to dedicated topics—'track-played', 'playlist-modified', 'user-followed'—with multiple services subscribing to relevant events. The event schema uses Protocol Buffers (protobuf) for efficient serialization and backward compatibility. Spotify chose Pub/Sub over Kafka primarily for operational simplicity and Google Cloud integration, though they accept the tradeoff of less control over partitioning and ordering guarantees. The system uses at-least-once delivery semantics, requiring downstream consumers to implement idempotent processing to handle potential duplicate events during retries.

sections.title: Backend For Frontend Pattern
sections.content: Spotify implements the Backend For Frontend (BFF) pattern, maintaining separate API layers for each client platform: iOS, Android, Web, Desktop, and connected devices like cars and smart speakers. Each BFF is owned by the corresponding platform team and optimized for that client's specific needs. For example, the mobile BFF aggressively batches requests and returns minimal payloads to reduce bandwidth on cellular connections, while the desktop BFF returns richer data structures since bandwidth isn't constrained. The BFF layer handles API composition, aggregating data from multiple microservices into a single client-optimized response. This prevents the 'chatty API' problem where mobile clients would need to make dozens of requests to render a single screen. Each BFF is implemented as a GraphQL gateway, allowing clients to specify exactly what data they need while the BFF efficiently fetches from underlying REST services.

sections.title: Real-Time Personalization Pipeline
sections.content: Spotify's personalization engine processes user listening history in real-time to power features like Discover Weekly, Daily Mix, and personalized home screens. The pipeline uses a lambda architecture combining batch and stream processing. Batch jobs running on Google Dataflow process complete listening history to train collaborative filtering models that identify similar users and tracks. Stream processing handles real-time signals—when a user plays a track, the event flows through Pub/Sub to a Flink job that updates user preference vectors in real-time. These vectors are stored in Bigtable, Google's NoSQL database, partitioned by user ID for fast lookup. The recommendation API queries Bigtable to retrieve user vectors, then uses approximate nearest neighbor search with vector embeddings to find similar tracks. The system balances exploration and exploitation using a contextual bandit approach, occasionally recommending unexpected content to discover new preferences while primarily serving known preferences.

sections.title: Audio Content Delivery Network
sections.content: Spotify's audio streaming infrastructure uses a hybrid P2P and CDN approach to deliver music efficiently. Audio files are encoded in multiple formats (Ogg Vorbis, AAC, MP3) at various bitrates (96kbps to 320kbps) to support different quality settings and device capabilities. The desktop client uses a proprietary P2P protocol where clients can serve cached audio chunks to nearby peers, reducing CDN load. Mobile clients use pure HTTP streaming from Google Cloud CDN to conserve battery. Audio files are chunked into 15-second segments, allowing the client to adapt bitrate based on network conditions. The CDN serves content from Google Cloud's edge locations with aggressive caching policies—popular tracks are cached for weeks while long-tail content is evicted more frequently. Spotify processes over 100 petabytes of audio streaming monthly, with the P2P protocol handling approximately 30% of desktop traffic, significantly reducing CDN costs.

sections.title: RINGPOP: Consistent Hashing for Dispatch
sections.content: Uber built RINGPOP, a consistent hashing framework on top of HashiCorp's SWIM gossip protocol, to distribute dispatch workload across hundreds of servers. Each dispatch server in a city is responsible for a portion of the geographic area, determined by consistent hashing of lat/lng coordinates. When a rider requests a ride, the request is routed to the server responsible for that location. RINGPOP handles server failures gracefully—when a node dies, its portion of the hash ring is automatically redistributed to remaining nodes within seconds. This approach provides horizontal scalability (add more servers to handle more requests) and fault tolerance without requiring centralized coordination. The consistent hashing ensures that each geographic region has a primary and multiple backup servers, allowing sub-second failover. RINGPOP processes over 50 million ride requests daily across all Uber markets globally.

sections.title: Dispatch Matching Algorithm
sections.content: The dispatch matching algorithm runs every second, evaluating all available drivers within a geographic area to find optimal assignments. The algorithm considers multiple factors: driver distance to pickup, driver direction and velocity, predicted pickup time, driver acceptance rate history, rider rating, and surge pricing zones. The optimization problem is formulated as a weighted bipartite matching, solved using the Hungarian algorithm with customized cost functions. For premium products like Uber Black, the algorithm also considers driver rating and vehicle year. The system handles edge cases like scheduled rides by pre-matching drivers and holding the assignment until the scheduled time approaches. During peak demand, the algorithm implements 'batching' where it waits 5-10 seconds to accumulate multiple requests before running matching, allowing it to find more optimal global assignments rather than greedy local decisions. This batching improved driver utilization by 15% without significantly impacting rider wait times.

sections.title: S2 Geometry for Geospatial Indexing
sections.content: Uber uses Google's S2 Geometry library to index and query driver locations at scale. S2 represents the Earth as a sphere and divides it into hierarchical cells using a Hilbert curve projection. Each cell has a unique 64-bit ID that preserves spatial locality—nearby cells have similar IDs, enabling efficient range queries. Uber stores driver locations in Redis with S2 cell IDs as keys, allowing fast queries like 'find all drivers within 2km of this location' by querying a small set of S2 cells that cover the desired region. The system uses S2 level 16 cells (approximately 200m x 200m) for driver location indexing and level 12 cells (approximately 3km x 3km) for city-level dispatch region boundaries. Driver location updates (streamed from mobile apps every 4 seconds) are written to Kafka, consumed by a service that updates Redis with TTL of 30 seconds. This architecture processes over 1 billion location updates per day with p99 query latency under 10ms.

sections.title: Dynamic Surge Pricing Engine
sections.content: Uber's surge pricing system uses real-time supply and demand data to dynamically adjust prices, incentivizing more drivers to go online during high-demand periods. The pricing engine runs every minute, calculating a surge multiplier for each geographic zone (typically S2 level 13 cells covering ~1km²). The calculation compares predicted demand (based on historical patterns, events, weather, and recent request rates) against available supply (number of active drivers). When demand exceeds supply by a threshold, surge activates with a multiplier that gradually increases to balance the market. The system uses a time-series database (M3DB) to track historical supply/demand patterns and predict future demand using ARIMA models. Surge multipliers are capped at 5x for rider experience reasons. The engine publishes surge zones to drivers via push notifications, creating a feedback loop where drivers relocate to high-surge areas. This mechanism has proven effective at reducing wait times during peak demand by up to 40%.

sections.title: Scaling Beyond Single PostgreSQL Instance
sections.content: Reddit's database architecture evolved from a single PostgreSQL instance to a sharded design as they scaled from millions to billions of posts and comments. The single database became the bottleneck around 2015 when write traffic exceeded 50,000 transactions per second during peak hours. Vertical scaling (larger instances) hit physical limits and became prohibitively expensive. The team chose horizontal sharding over other alternatives like NoSQL databases because they wanted to preserve PostgreSQL's ACID guarantees, complex query capabilities, and their existing expertise. The migration required 18 months of planning and execution, during which they built tooling to maintain consistency during the transition. The sharded architecture now handles over 300,000 writes per second across 200+ database shards, with room to scale further by adding more shards.

sections.title: Sharding by Thing ID
sections.content: Reddit shards their data by 'Thing ID'—their internal identifier for posts, comments, users, and votes. Each Thing ID is a 36-bit integer (allowing 68 billion unique IDs) combined with a 4-bit type identifier. The sharding function uses a hash of the Thing ID modulo the number of shards to determine placement. This scheme ensures even distribution of data across shards while maintaining the ability to locate any object with a single lookup. Related objects (like a post and its comments) can be co-located on the same shard by using derived IDs. User data is also sharded by user ID, meaning user profile operations hit a single shard. Cross-shard queries are avoided in hot paths—if a page requires data from multiple shards, the application layer fans out parallel queries and aggregates results. The sharding logic lives in a routing layer that translates Thing IDs to database connections, abstracting complexity from application code.

sections.title: Consistent Hashing for Shard Rebalancing
sections.content: Reddit uses consistent hashing to minimize data movement when adding new shards. In traditional modulo sharding, adding a shard would require moving approximately N/(N+1) of data (e.g., adding the 11th shard requires rebalancing 91% of data). Consistent hashing reduces this to approximately 1/N by assigning each shard multiple positions on a hash ring. When adding a new shard, only data from adjacent shards needs to move. Reddit's implementation uses 100 virtual nodes per physical shard on the hash ring, ensuring balanced distribution even with a small number of shards. Rebalancing operations are executed during low-traffic hours using a shadow-writing approach: new writes go to both old and new locations, historical data is backfilled asynchronously, then reads are cut over to the new shard, and finally old data is deleted. This zero-downtime migration process takes approximately 2 weeks per rebalancing operation.

sections.title: Operational Challenges and Solutions
sections.content: Sharding introduced several operational challenges. Schema migrations now require coordinated execution across hundreds of databases—Reddit built a migration orchestrator that runs DDL statements with exponential rollout, monitoring for errors at each stage. Backups are more complex, requiring consistent snapshots across shards; they use PostgreSQL streaming replication to replica servers, then take backups from replicas without impacting production. Analytics queries that previously ran on a single database now require federated queries or data warehouse export. Reddit uses a streaming pipeline (Kafka Connect) to replicate all shard data into a Redshift data warehouse for analytics workloads. Monitoring shifted from single-database metrics to aggregate metrics across shards—they track per-shard latency, error rates, and replication lag, alerting when any shard exceeds thresholds. Despite complexity, sharding enabled Reddit to scale while preserving PostgreSQL's benefits, proving that with proper tooling, sharded relational databases can handle massive scale.

sections.title: Metrics Ingestion Pipeline
sections.content: Datadog's metrics ingestion pipeline processes over 1 trillion data points per day from millions of hosts, containers, and services across customer infrastructure. The pipeline starts with the Datadog agent (open-source, written in Go) running on customer infrastructure, which collects system metrics, application metrics, logs, and traces. Agents aggregate metrics locally over 10-second intervals, then batch and compress data before sending via HTTPS to Datadog's intake API. The intake layer uses AWS Application Load Balancers fronting a fleet of EC2 instances running the intake service. Each intake node validates, enriches (adding tags like cloud provider, region, environment), and routes metrics to Kafka topics partitioned by metric type and customer account. This design provides horizontal scalability—they add intake capacity by launching more EC2 instances behind the load balancer. The intake layer handles traffic spikes of 3x average during incident scenarios when customers enable debug logging.

sections.title: Custom Time-Series Database
sections.content: Datadog built a custom time-series database optimized for high cardinality metrics with many tags. Unlike InfluxDB or Prometheus, which struggle with millions of unique time series, Datadog's database uses a columnar storage format with aggressive compression. Each metric is stored separately with timestamp, value, and tag columns. The database uses delta-of-delta encoding for timestamps (saving 90% space since most metrics arrive at regular intervals) and Gorilla compression for float values (achieving 12x compression on typical metrics). Tags are stored in a separate inverted index that maps tag values to time series IDs, enabling fast filtering queries like 'show CPU usage where host=prod AND region=us-east-1'. The database is sharded by metric name and customer account, with each shard handling 10-50 million data points per second. Data is retained at full resolution for 15 months, then downsampled to hourly granularity for long-term storage. This architecture provides sub-second query response times even over year-long time ranges.

sections.title: Distributed Query Engine
sections.content: Datadog's query engine uses a distributed architecture to handle complex aggregation queries across petabytes of time-series data. When a user creates a dashboard or runs an alert query, the query is parsed into an execution plan that identifies which shards contain relevant data. The query coordinator fans out sub-queries to shard workers in parallel, each worker reading from local SSDs and performing partial aggregations. Workers apply filters early (tag filtering, time range), minimizing data shuffling. Results are streamed back to the coordinator which performs final aggregations and applies mathematical functions. The system uses speculative execution—if a worker is slow, the coordinator sends the same sub-query to a backup worker and uses whichever responds first. Query results are cached in Redis with cache keys that include metric names, tags, time range, and aggregation function. The cache hit rate exceeds 60% for dashboards, dramatically reducing query load. This architecture enables Datadog to handle 10 million queries per hour with p95 latency under 2 seconds.

sections.title: Real-Time Alerting System
sections.content: Datadog's alerting system evaluates millions of alert rules every minute against incoming metrics. The architecture uses a stream processing approach rather than periodic polling. As metrics flow through Kafka, a Flink-based alerting service consumes metrics and evaluates alert conditions in real-time. Each alert rule (e.g., 'CPU > 80% for 5 minutes') is compiled into a stateful Flink operator that maintains a sliding window of recent values. When thresholds are breached, the operator emits an alert event. Alert events flow to a deduplication service that groups related alerts (same host, same condition) and applies hysteresis to prevent flapping. The notification router then sends alerts via configured channels—email, PagerDuty, Slack, webhooks. The system handles alert routing for over 1 million active monitors, delivering notifications with p99 latency under 60 seconds from when the threshold breach occurs. Priority alerts use a separate fast-path pipeline with guaranteed 10-second notification delivery.

sections.title: Visual Embedding Generation
sections.content: Pinterest's visual search uses convolutional neural networks to generate high-dimensional embeddings (2048 dimensions) for every image on their platform. The embedding model is a modified ResNet-50 architecture trained on 5 billion pins using a triplet loss function that ensures visually similar images have nearby embeddings in vector space. The training data includes implicit signals (users saving similar pins together) and explicit signals (user-reported similar items). The model is retrained weekly on new data to capture emerging visual trends. Image processing happens asynchronously after pin creation: the image is downloaded, resized to multiple resolutions, passed through the CNN, and the resulting embedding vector is stored in a specialized vector database. Pinterest processes over 10 million new images daily through this pipeline using a combination of GPUs on AWS EC2 P3 instances for embedding generation and CPU instances for ancillary processing.

sections.title: Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
sections.content: Finding similar images requires searching billions of embedding vectors, a computationally expensive operation. Pinterest uses Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) graphs for approximate nearest neighbor search. The HNSW index is built by connecting each vector to its k nearest neighbors at multiple hierarchical levels, creating a structure that can be traversed efficiently. Queries start at the top level and greedily traverse towards nearest neighbors, dropping to lower levels until reaching the bottom layer. This provides logarithmic search complexity with high recall—Pinterest achieves 95% recall with searches completing in under 50ms. The index is partitioned across multiple servers with each partition containing approximately 100 million vectors. Query requests are fanned out to all partitions in parallel, each partition returns its top-k results, and the query coordinator merges results. The HNSW indices are rebuilt nightly from updated embeddings and atomically swapped with production indices to incorporate new pins and retrained models.

sections.title: Search Ranking and Personalization
sections.content: After retrieving candidate pins via vector similarity, Pinterest applies a sophisticated ranking model that personalizes results for each user. The ranking model is a gradient boosted decision tree (XGBoost) trained on billions of user interaction events. Features include visual similarity score, pin quality signals (saves, clicks, closeups), content freshness, user historical preferences, contextual signals (time of day, device type, search query), and social signals (pins from users you follow). The model predicts the probability a user will engage with each pin (save, click, closeup), and pins are ranked by predicted engagement. The ranking model is A/B tested continuously with multiple models serving different traffic percentages. Model updates are deployed via feature flags with gradual rollout—a new model starts at 1% traffic, increases to 10%, 50%, and finally 100% over several days while monitoring engagement metrics. This careful deployment process ensures that model regressions are caught before impacting all users.

sections.title: Object Detection for Shop the Look
sections.content: Pinterest's 'Shop the Look' feature allows users to identify and purchase products within images. This requires object detection models that identify individual objects (shoes, furniture, clothing) within pins. Pinterest uses Mask R-CNN models trained on proprietary datasets labeled with product categories and bounding boxes. The model runs inference on every new pin, detecting objects and their locations. For each detected object, Pinterest generates a separate embedding and searches against a catalog database of shoppable products to find exact or similar matches. The catalog contains 100+ million products from retail partners, each with embeddings generated from product images. Matching happens in real-time as users interact with pins—when a user taps a hotspot, Pinterest searches the catalog and returns purchasable products ranked by visual similarity and price. This pipeline processes 50,000 shopping queries per second during peak hours, with p99 latency under 300ms including object detection, embedding generation, catalog search, and ranking.

sections.title: Handling 10x Traffic Spikes
sections.content: Flipkart's Big Billion Day flash sales generate traffic spikes 10-20x normal levels, with millions of users attempting to purchase limited inventory simultaneously. Traditional architectures would collapse under this load. Flipkart pre-scales infrastructure by 5x before the event, launching thousands of additional EC2 instances days in advance. They use AWS Auto Scaling with scheduled actions to gradually ramp capacity, avoiding sudden scaling that might trigger infrastructure issues. Static assets (images, JavaScript, CSS) are served from CloudFront CDN with aggressive caching (7-day TTL) and pre-warmed caches populated via automated crawlers hitting all product pages hours before the sale. The backend API layer uses horizontal scaling with stateless servers behind Application Load Balancers. Database read load is offloaded to 20+ read replicas with eventual consistency acceptable for most queries. Despite this preparation, some bottlenecks emerge unpredictably, requiring real-time capacity adjustments during the event.

sections.title: Virtual Waiting Room Queue System
sections.content: To prevent stampeding the checkout flow, Flipkart implements a virtual waiting room using a distributed queue system built on Redis. When flash sale inventory is limited to 10,000 units but 1 million users are competing, the queue system meters traffic to downstream systems. Users entering the site during high load are placed in a queue with a position number and estimated wait time. The queue is implemented as a Redis Sorted Set with scores based on arrival timestamp, ensuring first-come-first-served fairness. A dequeuer service periodically admits users from the queue to the shopping flow at a controlled rate (e.g., 1,000 users per second). The admission rate is dynamically adjusted based on downstream system health metrics—if checkout service latency increases, admission rate decreases. This backpressure mechanism prevents cascading failures. The queue UI updates in real-time via WebSocket connections showing the user's current position. This approach maintains system stability while providing a fair experience, even if some users must wait several minutes before purchasing.

sections.title: Distributed Inventory Management
sections.content: Flash sale inventory management requires real-time accuracy while handling concurrent updates from millions of users. Flipkart uses a two-phase approach: optimistic checking followed by pessimistic locking. When a user adds a flash sale item to cart, the system performs a fast Redis read to check available inventory. If inventory exists, the item is temporarily reserved in Redis with a 10-minute TTL. This prevents overselling while giving users time to complete checkout. When the user confirms purchase, the system acquires a pessimistic lock in PostgreSQL (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) to decrement inventory in the source-of-truth database. If the lock acquisition times out (indicating high contention), the transaction is retried with exponential backoff. The Redis layer caches inventory counts with 1-second TTL, refreshed by a background job that reads from PostgreSQL. This architecture provides sub-100ms inventory checks for 99% of requests while guaranteeing no overselling via the database lock. The system handles 100,000 inventory checks per second during peak flash sale moments.

sections.title: Real-Time Observability During Sales
sections.content: During flash sales, Flipkart's engineering team monitors dozens of real-time dashboards showing system health, business metrics, and user experience. The observability stack uses Prometheus for metrics collection from all services, with custom exporters for business metrics like checkout conversion rate and inventory availability. Metrics are visualized in Grafana dashboards with panels showing request rates, error rates, latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99), database connection pool utilization, and queue lengths. Alerts fire when key metrics exceed thresholds: p99 latency > 2 seconds, error rate > 0.5%, or queue wait time > 10 minutes. The team uses distributed tracing with Jaeger to diagnose performance issues in real-time—when a user reports a slow checkout, engineers can pull up the trace showing exactly which service calls were slow. Logs are aggregated in Elasticsearch with structured logging (JSON format) enabling fast queries during incidents. This comprehensive observability enabled the team to execute 30+ real-time optimizations during a recent flash sale, maintaining system stability while processing 5 million orders in 24 hours.

sections.title: Need for Async Processing at Scale
sections.content: Facebook built FOQS (Facebook Online Queueing System) to handle asynchronous task processing at massive scale. Many Facebook features require async processing: photo uploads must be resized and stored in multiple resolutions, videos need transcoding, news feed stories trigger notifications to potentially millions of users, and posts must be analyzed for policy violations. Synchronous processing of these tasks in the request path would make the product unusably slow. Early Facebook used MySQL as a task queue (polling a jobs table), but this approach failed to scale beyond 10,000 tasks per second due to database contention on the queue table. FOQS was designed to handle millions of tasks per second with low latency, high availability, and exactly-once execution semantics. The system has evolved to process over 100 billion tasks per day across thousands of queue types.

sections.title: Sharded Queue Architecture
sections.content: FOQS uses a sharded architecture where queues are distributed across thousands of servers. Each queue (e.g., 'photo-resize-queue', 'notification-delivery-queue') is split into 100-1000 shards distributed across the server fleet. Producers enqueue tasks by hashing a shard key (e.g., user ID) to determine the target shard, then sending the task via Thrift RPC to the corresponding FOQS server. The server appends the task to an in-memory buffer backed by a write-ahead log on local SSD for durability. Consumers (worker services) connect to FOQS servers and long-poll for tasks. When tasks are available, FOQS returns a batch of up to 100 tasks. The consumer processes tasks and acknowledges completion, causing FOQS to delete the tasks. This architecture provides horizontal scalability—adding queue capacity means deploying more FOQS servers. The sharding ensures that tasks for a single user are processed in order (FIFO within shard), which is critical for features like photo album uploads.

sections.title: Exactly-Once Delivery Guarantees
sections.content: FOQS provides exactly-once processing semantics using a combination of idempotency keys and visibility timeouts. When a task is enqueued, the producer provides an idempotency key (usually a deterministic hash of the task parameters). FOQS maintains a recent history of completed idempotency keys in a bloom filter and Cassandra database. If a duplicate task is submitted (e.g., due to producer retry), FOQS detects the duplicate via the idempotency key and returns success without re-enqueueing. When a consumer dequeues a task, it becomes invisible to other consumers for a configurable visibility timeout (default 5 minutes). If the consumer crashes or times out, the task becomes visible again and can be processed by another consumer. This provides at-least-once delivery. Combined with the idempotency key check, the system achieves exactly-once semantics. Consumers must implement idempotent processing to handle the rare duplicate scenario if visibility timeout is too short.

sections.title: Priority Queues and Rate Limiting
sections.content: FOQS supports priority levels (0-15) allowing critical tasks to be processed before background tasks. Within each shard, tasks are stored in priority-ordered lists. When a consumer requests tasks, FOQS scans from highest to lowest priority and returns tasks from the first non-empty priority level. This ensures time-sensitive tasks like real-time notifications preempt batch processing tasks like data analytics. FOQS also implements per-queue and per-consumer rate limiting to prevent queue starvation and resource exhaustion. Each queue has a configurable maximum throughput (tasks per second), enforced using a token bucket algorithm. If enqueueing would exceed the rate limit, the request is rejected with backpressure signaling. Similarly, consumers have rate limits preventing a single consumer from monopolizing queue capacity. These mechanisms ensure fairness and prevent scenarios where one queue or consumer degrades the entire system.

sections.title: Kafka as Central Nervous System
sections.content: LinkedIn created Apache Kafka in 2011 to power their real-time analytics platform, and it remains central to their architecture today. Every user action—profile views, post impressions, searches, messages, connection requests—generates an event published to Kafka topics. The platform processes over 7 trillion messages per day across 4,000+ Kafka topics. Kafka clusters are organized by data center and business domain, with the largest cluster containing 3,000 brokers handling 20 million messages per second at peak. Topics use partitioning for parallelism—the 'profile-view' topic has 1,000 partitions allowing 1,000 consumers to process events concurrently. Retention policies vary by topic: real-time metrics topics retain 24 hours of data, while audit logs retain 90 days. Kafka's replication (typically 3x) provides fault tolerance, with brokers spread across availability zones. LinkedIn's scale pushed Kafka's limits, leading to optimizations like tiered storage (moving old data to S3) and KRaft mode (removing ZooKeeper dependency) now available in open-source Kafka.

sections.title: Apache Samza Stream Processing
sections.content: LinkedIn built Apache Samza for stateful stream processing of Kafka events. Samza jobs consume events from Kafka topics, apply transformations, maintain local state, and produce results to output topics. For example, a 'profile-view-counter' Samza job consumes profile view events, maintains a counter per profile (stored in embedded RocksDB), and outputs updated counts to a 'profile-view-counts' topic. The local state provides fast reads (no network calls) while RocksDB's compaction keeps memory usage bounded. Samza checkpoints state to Kafka topics periodically, enabling recovery after failures—when a job restarts, it restores state from the last checkpoint. Samza scales horizontally by assigning Kafka partitions to Samza containers (JVM processes). LinkedIn runs thousands of Samza jobs processing billions of events per second collectively. Use cases include real-time metrics aggregation, fraud detection, notification triggers, and materialized view maintenance for serving systems.

sections.title: Apache Pinot for User-Facing Analytics
sections.content: LinkedIn built Apache Pinot, a real-time OLAP database, to power user-facing analytics like 'Who Viewed Your Profile' and company page analytics. Pinot ingests events from Kafka topics in real-time, indexes them for fast aggregation queries, and serves queries with p99 latency under 100ms at LinkedIn's scale. Data is organized into tables with segment-based architecture—each segment contains data for a time range and is immutable once sealed. Segments use columnar storage with dictionary encoding and inverted indexes for fast filtering. Pinot uses a scatter-gather query model: the broker receives a query, scatters it to all servers containing relevant segments, each server processes its segments in parallel, and the broker gathers and merges results. Pinot handles over 200,000 queries per second at LinkedIn with most queries aggregating billions of records. The system uses time-based retention, automatically deleting old segments to bound storage. Pinot's real-time ingestion combined with sub-second query latency makes it suitable for interactive user-facing dashboards.

sections.title: ThirdEye Anomaly Detection
sections.content: LinkedIn's ThirdEye system detects anomalies in time-series metrics by applying machine learning to thousands of business metrics tracked in Pinot. ThirdEye runs scheduled detection pipelines every 15 minutes, querying Pinot for recent metric values (e.g., search query rate, profile view count, message send rate) and comparing against expected values predicted by time-series models. The system uses multiple detection algorithms including ARIMA forecasting, Holt-Winters exponential smoothing, and ensemble models combining multiple approaches. When an anomaly is detected (actual value deviates from predicted by more than 3 standard deviations), ThirdEye generates an alert. The system performs automatic root cause analysis by analyzing correlated metrics and dimensions to identify which user segment or platform contributed to the anomaly. Engineers receive alerts via Slack or email with suggested root causes. ThirdEye reduces false positives by learning from user feedback—when engineers mark an alert as false positive, the system retrains models to avoid similar alerts. This closed-loop system has reduced alert fatigue while catching critical issues like sudden drops in user engagement.

sections.title: Custom Routing Engine
sections.content: Grab built a custom routing engine to calculate optimal routes for ride-hailing and delivery across Southeast Asia's complex road networks. The engine uses OpenStreetMap (OSM) data augmented with proprietary road data from driver GPS traces. Grab processes billions of GPS coordinates monthly to identify new roads, traffic patterns, and road closures not reflected in OSM. The routing graph contains 100+ million nodes and 500+ million edges across their operating regions. Edge weights are dynamically calculated based on current traffic conditions from real-time driver locations, historical traffic patterns by time-of-day and day-of-week, and road attributes like speed limits and turn restrictions. The routing algorithm is a customized A* search with several optimizations: bidirectional search (searching from both start and destination simultaneously), contraction hierarchies (pre-computing shortcuts for faster searches), and edge pruning (eliminating obviously suboptimal paths early). Queries complete in under 500ms for 99% of routes despite the graph size.

sections.title: Machine Learning ETA Prediction
sections.content: Grab's ETA prediction system combines routing engine output with machine learning models that account for real-world delays. The routing engine provides a baseline ETA based on road network and traffic, but real journeys have additional variance from driver behavior, passenger no-shows, navigation errors, parking difficulty, and weather impacts. Grab trains gradient boosted tree models (LightGBM) on historical trip data to predict actual travel time. Features include route distance, number of turns, traffic level, time of day, weather conditions, driver experience, vehicle type, and historical delay patterns for specific road segments. The model outputs a probability distribution over possible travel times rather than a point estimate, allowing the system to show confidence intervals. For example, an ETA might be '15 minutes ±3 minutes with 90% confidence'. The model is retrained daily on the previous week's trips and deployed to production via A/B testing. Current models achieve mean absolute error under 2 minutes for 80% of trips.

sections.title: S2 Geometry for Location Indexing
sections.content: Like Uber, Grab uses Google's S2 Geometry library for geospatial indexing, but with Southeast Asia-specific optimizations. S2 cells naturally adapt to varying densities—urban areas like Singapore use smaller cells (level 16: ~200m²) while rural areas use larger cells (level 12: ~10km²). Grab pre-computes cell level assignments for their entire operating region and stores this mapping in their geospatial service. Driver locations are indexed in Redis Cluster with S2 cell ID as the key and driver ID as the value. Each driver's location is indexed in multiple overlapping cells to handle queries that span cell boundaries. When searching for nearby drivers, the system queries all S2 cells that cover the search radius, unions the results, and filters by precise distance calculation. Redis Cluster provides horizontal scaling and automatic sharding. Grab processes 50,000 location updates per second and 100,000 proximity queries per second with p95 latency under 15ms. The S2-based architecture proved essential for Southeast Asia's geography with its numerous islands, complex coastlines, and varying development densities.

sections.title: GPS Map Matching Algorithm
sections.content: Grab's map matching algorithm corrects noisy GPS coordinates to snap them to actual road locations. Raw GPS from smartphones has 10-50 meter error, especially in urban canyons where tall buildings cause multipath interference. Map matching uses a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) approach where the hidden state is the true road location and the observation is the GPS coordinate. The algorithm considers multiple candidate road segments near each GPS point, then finds the most likely sequence of road segments that explains the GPS trajectory. Likelihood considers GPS measurement error (closer candidates are more likely), route continuity (prefer sequences connected by roads), and heading consistency (GPS heading should match road direction). The Viterbi algorithm finds the maximum likelihood path efficiently. Grab enhanced the basic algorithm with additional constraints: prefer roads with traffic (from other drivers), penalize unlikely maneuvers (e.g., U-turns on highways), and use phone sensors (accelerometer, gyroscope) to detect stopped vehicles. Map matching improves location accuracy from 25m median error (raw GPS) to 5m median error, crucial for features like precise pickup locations and lane-level navigation.

sections.title: Multi-Model Serving Architecture
sections.content: Perplexity serves multiple LLMs concurrently to balance cost, latency, and quality. Their architecture uses a router model that selects which LLM to use for each query based on query complexity and user tier. Simple factual queries go to smaller, faster models (7B parameters, 100ms latency) while complex reasoning queries use larger models (70B+ parameters, 2-5s latency). The serving infrastructure uses NVIDIA Triton Inference Server on AWS EC2 P4d instances (8x A100 GPUs per instance). Models are loaded into GPU memory with TensorRT optimization, achieving 2-3x throughput improvement over naive PyTorch inference. Perplexity uses continuous batching (also called iteration-level scheduling) where inference requests are batched dynamically during generation rather than waiting for full batch assembly. This reduces average latency by 40% compared to static batching while maintaining high GPU utilization. The system handles 10,000+ queries per minute during peak hours across 100+ GPU instances.

sections.title: Aggressive Response Caching
sections.content: LLM inference is expensive—$0.50 per 1M tokens for a 70B parameter model. Perplexity reduces costs dramatically through aggressive caching at multiple levels. The first level is exact query caching: if the exact same query has been answered recently, return the cached response. This handles 15-20% of queries (popular questions like 'What is the capital of France?'). The second level is semantic caching using embedding similarity: queries with similar embeddings (cosine similarity > 0.95) return the same cached response. This adds another 10% cache hit rate. The third level is partial caching where common query prefixes are cached to accelerate generation—for example, 'How do I' queries share common reasoning patterns. Caches are stored in Redis Cluster with TTL of 24 hours for exact matches and 1 hour for semantic matches. Cache keys for semantic matching use approximate nearest neighbor search with FAISS indexes. The multi-level caching strategy achieves an overall 35% cache hit rate, reducing inference costs by over $1M monthly while maintaining response quality.

sections.title: Real-Time Web Retrieval Pipeline
sections.content: Perplexity's core differentiator is real-time web retrieval augmentation. When a query arrives, the system first generates search queries using a specialized LLM prompt ('Generate 3 search queries to answer: {user_query}'). These search queries execute against their web search index (built on Elasticsearch with 100B+ crawled documents) and external APIs (Bing, Google). The top 10 results are fetched, and full HTML content is downloaded concurrently. Content extraction uses Mozilla's Readability library to strip ads/navigation and keep main content. The extracted text (limited to 5,000 tokens per source) is chunked and ranked by relevance using a cross-encoder model that scores query-document pairs. The top 5 most relevant chunks (approximately 3,000 tokens total) are injected into the LLM prompt as context. The entire retrieval pipeline completes in under 2 seconds, running in parallel with the router model selection. This architecture ensures responses are grounded in current information while maintaining conversational latency.

sections.title: Citation Attribution System
sections.content: Perplexity generates inline citations linking claims to source documents, differentiating them from generic chatbots. The citation system works by having the LLM generate responses with special tokens indicating citation points: 'Paris is the capital of France[1].' During post-processing, the system extracts these citation tokens and maps them to source documents. The mapping uses sentence embedding similarity—each claim is embedded and matched against sentences from the retrieved documents to find the source. This automatic attribution achieves 90% accuracy verified by human raters. For the remaining 10%, a fallback attribute to the most relevant document. Citations are rendered as clickable footnotes with document previews. The system tracks citation usage analytics to identify which sources are most valuable and prioritize them in future retrievals. This approach addresses a critical weakness of pure LLMs (hallucination/unverifiable claims) while adding minimal latency (<100ms post-processing). The citation system has been crucial for user trust and has led to 70% of users clicking on at least one citation per session.

sections.title: Why Serverless for Banking
sections.content: Nubank, Brazil's largest digital bank with 90+ million customers, built their core banking platform on serverless architecture using AWS Lambda and Clojure. This unconventional choice for a bank was driven by several factors: rapid scaling requirements (growing from 0 to 90M users in 10 years), cost efficiency (pay-per-request vs. paying for idle capacity), and reduced operational burden (no server patching or capacity planning). Banking workloads have extreme spikes—paydays see 10x traffic increases for hours, then drop back. Serverless handles this naturally by auto-scaling to thousands of concurrent executions within seconds. Nubank's architecture uses event-driven patterns extensively with Lambda functions triggered by API Gateway requests, SQS messages, DynamoDB streams, and scheduled events. The team reports that serverless reduced their infrastructure team size by 60% compared to traditional architectures, allowing engineers to focus on business logic rather than ops.

sections.title: Function Design and Cold Start Optimization
sections.content: Nubank's Lambda functions are written in Clojure, compiled to JVM bytecode. Each function is small and focused—average function has 200 lines of code and does one thing well. This follows the microservices philosophy at the function level. Cold start latency (time to spin up a new function instance) is critical for user-facing APIs. JVM cold starts typically take 2-5 seconds, unacceptable for banking apps. Nubank optimized cold starts to under 1 second through several techniques: reducing dependency size (uber-jar is <20MB), using AWS Lambda SnapStart (takes snapshot of initialized JVM and restores from snapshot), lazy loading of dependencies (only load what's needed for current execution), and provisioned concurrency for latency-sensitive functions. The provisioned concurrency feature pre-warms function instances, eliminating cold starts for critical paths like login and transaction authorization. Nubank keeps 500-1000 instances warm for their hottest functions, costing $5K/month but guaranteeing sub-100ms p99 latency.

sections.title: DynamoDB as Primary Database
sections.content: Nubank uses DynamoDB as their primary operational database for most customer-facing features. DynamoDB's serverless scaling model (pay per request, auto-scales to millions of requests per second) aligns with their Lambda architecture. The data model uses single-table design where multiple entity types share one table with partition keys that enable fast access patterns. For example, the customer table uses composite keys: 'USER#123456' (partition) and 'PROFILE' or 'TRANSACTION#2025-01-15' (sort key), allowing efficient queries for user profile and recent transactions. DynamoDB Streams enable event-driven architectures—when a transaction is written to DynamoDB, a stream event triggers Lambda functions for notifications, fraud detection, and analytics. For relational query needs (complex joins and analytics), Nubank uses DynamoDB to Aurora PostgreSQL replication via Lambda functions that consume DynamoDB streams and write to Aurora. This hybrid approach provides the scalability of DynamoDB for OLTP workloads while enabling SQL analytics on replicated data.

sections.title: Security and Compliance in Serverless
sections.content: Banking regulations require stringent security controls. Nubank implements defense-in-depth with multiple security layers. Network isolation uses VPC Lambda functions that access databases through private subnets with no internet access. Secrets management uses AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation every 30 days. All Lambda functions run with minimal IAM permissions following the principle of least privilege—each function has a unique role with permissions scoped to exactly what it needs. Encryption is ubiquitous: data at rest (DynamoDB, S3) uses AWS KMS encryption, data in transit uses TLS 1.3, and sensitive data is additionally encrypted at the application layer. Audit logging captures every API call and data access with CloudTrail and custom application logs sent to S3 for long-term retention (7 years, per Brazilian banking regulations). Compliance automation uses Lambda functions to continuously verify security controls—functions run hourly to check for misconfigurations like overly permissive IAM policies or disabled encryption. This serverless security architecture passed multiple audits by Brazilian banking regulators, proving that serverless can meet stringent compliance requirements.

sections.title: Radical Microservices Decomposition
sections.content: Zalando, Europe's largest online fashion retailer, operates one of the most aggressive microservices architectures with over 1,500 independently deployable services. The decomposition followed domain-driven design with bounded contexts around business capabilities: catalog (product information), inventory (stock levels), pricing (dynamic pricing), cart (shopping basket), checkout (payment processing), fulfillment (order processing), and customer (profiles and preferences). Each team owns multiple services end-to-end including development, deployment, and operations. Services communicate exclusively via REST APIs or event streams—no shared databases. This autonomy enables fast development (teams deploy independently 50+ times per day) but introduces distributed system challenges. Service discovery uses Kubernetes DNS, API gateway handles external traffic routing, and circuit breakers prevent cascading failures. The architecture scales to handle 100 million visits per month and 50,000 orders per day.

sections.title: Skipper API Gateway
sections.content: Zalando built Skipper, an HTTP router and API gateway handling all external and internal traffic. Skipper runs as Kubernetes pods (100+ instances) behind AWS Network Load Balancers, processing over 200,000 requests per second at peak. Routing rules are defined in Git and deployed continuously—when a team updates their service's routing configuration, the change propagates to all Skipper instances within 30 seconds via Kubernetes ConfigMaps. Skipper provides sophisticated routing capabilities: weighted traffic splitting for blue-green deployments, shadow traffic copying to test new versions, rate limiting per client, authentication via OAuth2, request/response transformation, and automatic retries with exponential backoff. The gateway implements health checks and circuit breakers—if a backend service's error rate exceeds 10%, Skipper automatically stops routing traffic and returns cached responses or fallback data. Skipper's design is stateless (routing rules are config, no database), enabling horizontal scaling and fast rollouts. The team open-sourced Skipper, and it's used by other large-scale European tech companies.

sections.title: Nakadi Event Streaming Platform
sections.content: Zalando built Nakadi, an event streaming platform that provides a REST API over Apache Kafka. Nakadi abstracts Kafka's complexity, allowing teams to publish and consume events via simple HTTP requests without learning Kafka clients, ZooKeeper, or consumer group management. Events follow a standard schema (JSON with event type, metadata, and payload) enforced by JSON Schema validation. Event types are versioned with compatibility rules ensuring backward compatibility. For example, the 'order.placed' event type defines fields like order_id, customer_id, and items. Consumers subscribe via Server-Sent Events (SSE), receiving a stream of events over long-lived HTTP connections. Nakadi handles Kafka consumer group management, offset tracking, and rebalancing transparently. The platform processes over 1 billion events per day across 500+ event types. Zalando uses events for cross-service communication (publish-subscribe), data pipeline ingestion, and audit logging. The event-driven architecture enables loose coupling—services don't need to know about downstream consumers, they just publish events and move on.

sections.title: Database Per Service Pattern
sections.content: Zalando enforces database-per-service pattern where each microservice owns its database schema and other services cannot directly access it. This provides loose coupling and independent scaling but introduces challenges for cross-service queries. For example, displaying order history with product details requires joining order data (order service database) with product data (catalog service database). Zalando solves this through several patterns: API composition (order service calls catalog service API to fetch product details), data replication (catalog service publishes product update events, order service consumes and maintains a local denormalized copy), and CQRS (separate read models optimized for queries, updated via events). Most services use PostgreSQL for primary storage due to strong consistency, ACID guarantees, and powerful query capabilities. Some services use Redis for caching, Elasticsearch for search, and S3 for blob storage. The database-per-service pattern enables teams to choose appropriate data stores and schema designs for their domain without coordination, though it requires careful event-driven integration.

sections.title: Elo Rating System for Desirability
sections.content: Tinder uses a modified Elo rating system (similar to chess rankings) to score user attractiveness and match desirability. Each user starts with an Elo score of 1000. When user A swipes right on user B, nothing happens immediately. If user B also swipes right (creating a match), both users gain Elo points—but the amount depends on relative scores. If a high-Elo user swipes right on a low-Elo user, the low-Elo user gains many points (surprising approval from attractive person) while the high-Elo user gains few points. If similar-Elo users match, both gain moderate points. Conversely, left swipes decrease the rejected user's score slightly. This creates a dynamic ranking where users are scored based on their match rate and the quality of people who match with them. The Elo score influences who appears in your card stack—Tinder shows profiles of similar Elo scores to create balanced matches. The system processes 1.6 billion swipes per day, updating Elo scores in near real-time (within 1 minute) using a stream processing pipeline.

sections.title: Real-Time Card Stack Generation
sections.content: Generating the card stack (profiles to swipe on) requires real-time computation balancing multiple factors: geographic proximity, Elo score similarity, age preferences, gender preferences, and freshness (avoid showing the same profiles repeatedly). When a user opens the app, Tinder queries a candidate pool of 500-1000 users matching basic criteria (location within 50 miles, age within preferences, appropriate gender). This query hits a geo-partitioned MongoDB cluster indexed by location (GeoJSON) and user attributes. The candidate pool is then ranked by a scoring function combining Elo similarity (prefer similar scores), last active time (prefer recently active users), and randomization (prevent staleness). The top 50 profiles are prefetched from image CDN and sent to the mobile app. As the user swipes, the app maintains a local buffer of 10 upcoming profiles while requesting the next batch asynchronously. This streaming approach ensures smooth UX without waiting for batch loads. The card stack is personalized using machine learning models that predict swipe probability based on user history, but the Elo-based filtering significantly reduces the search space making real-time scoring feasible.

sections.title: Real-Time Messaging Infrastructure
sections.content: Tinder's chat infrastructure handles 10+ billion messages per day with sub-second delivery latency. The architecture uses WebSocket connections between mobile apps and a WebSocket gateway layer (implemented with Socket.io on Node.js). When users open a chat, the app establishes a WebSocket connection to the gateway. The gateway subscribes to relevant message channels in Redis Pub/Sub, one channel per conversation. When user A sends a message to user B, the message is written to MongoDB (messages table, indexed by conversation_id and timestamp) and published to the conversation's Redis channel. The gateway forwards the message over WebSocket to any connected clients. If user B is offline, the message is stored in MongoDB and delivered when they reconnect. Push notifications trigger for offline users using Firebase Cloud Messaging. The system uses horizontal scaling with sticky sessions—each user's WebSocket connection pins to a specific gateway instance via load balancer session affinity. Redis Cluster provides pub/sub scalability across 100+ gateway instances. The architecture provides at-most-once delivery (messages aren't duplicated) but ensures durability via MongoDB persistence.

sections.title: Image Processing and CDN
sections.content: Profile photos are critical to Tinder's UX, requiring fast loading and high quality. When users upload photos, the images are processed through a pipeline: uploaded to S3, then processed by Lambda functions that detect inappropriate content (using AWS Rekognition for nudity detection), generate multiple resolutions (thumbnail 150x150, medium 600x600, full 1200x1200), compress using WebP format (40% smaller than JPEG with comparable quality), and extract dominant colors for placeholder backgrounds. Processed images are stored in S3 and served via CloudFront CDN with aggressive caching (30-day TTL). The mobile app requests appropriate resolution based on device and network conditions—cellular connections get medium resolution, WiFi gets full resolution. For premium users with 'Super Likes' feature, the app prefetches full-resolution photos of top 10 card stack profiles during idle moments to ensure instant display when swiping. The image pipeline processes 500,000 new photos daily and serves 10 billion image requests per day from CDN edge locations worldwide, achieving 95% cache hit rate and p50 load time under 200ms.

sections.title: Continuous Batching for Throughput
sections.content: OpenAI serves GPT models using continuous batching (also called iteration-level scheduling), a technique that dramatically improves GPU utilization and throughput. Traditional batching waits for a fixed batch of requests before starting inference, then processes all requests together. This wastes GPU cycles when sequences finish at different times—a short completion like 'Yes' finishes in 5 tokens while a long completion generates 500 tokens, but GPU sits idle waiting for the batch to complete. Continuous batching inserts new requests into the batch as soon as any sequence finishes, maintaining full GPU utilization. OpenAI's implementation uses a priority queue where requests are prioritized by wait time, ensuring fair scheduling. The batch size dynamically adjusts based on sequence lengths—shorter sequences allow larger batches (up to 512 sequences) while longer sequences use smaller batches (64-128 sequences) to fit in GPU memory. This approach increased throughput by 3-5x compared to static batching while reducing average latency by 30%, critical for serving millions of requests daily.

sections.title: KV Cache Optimization
sections.content: Transformer models like GPT require storing key-value (KV) caches for all previous tokens in the sequence to avoid recomputing attention. For a GPT-4 scale model (trillions of parameters) generating 500 tokens, the KV cache can exceed 10GB per request, quickly exhausting GPU memory. OpenAI uses several optimizations: quantization (storing KV caches in INT8 instead of FP32, reducing memory by 4x with minimal quality impact), offloading (moving older KV cache to CPU RAM when GPU memory is tight, fetching back when needed), and recomputation (for extremely memory-constrained scenarios, recompute KV cache instead of storing it, trading compute for memory). For multi-turn conversations, OpenAI caches KV for the conversation history across requests—when a user sends a follow-up message, the system retrieves cached KV for previous turns instead of reprocessing them. This reduces latency by 40-60% for multi-turn dialogues. The KV cache is sharded across multiple GPUs when model size requires tensor parallelism, requiring careful synchronization to maintain coherence.

sections.title: Tensor and Pipeline Parallelism
sections.content: GPT-4 scale models don't fit on a single GPU, requiring distributed inference across multiple GPUs. OpenAI uses a combination of tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism. Tensor parallelism splits individual layers across GPUs—for example, a 16,384-dimensional attention layer is split across 8 GPUs with each handling 2,048 dimensions. This requires all-reduce communication after each layer to aggregate results, introducing synchronization overhead. Pipeline parallelism splits the model vertically into stages with different layers on different GPUs—layers 1-20 on GPU 0, layers 21-40 on GPU 1, etc. Sequences flow through stages in a pipeline, allowing concurrent processing of multiple requests. The challenge is balancing pipeline stages to avoid bottlenecks—OpenAI uses profiling to assign layers to stages such that execution time is similar across stages. For GPT-4, they use 8-way tensor parallelism within nodes (8 GPUs connected via NVLink) and 16-way pipeline parallelism across nodes (connected via InfiniBand). This hybrid approach balances communication overhead with parallelism benefits.

sections.title: Speculative Decoding for Latency
sections.content: Autoregressive generation (generating one token at a time) is inherently sequential, limiting parallelism. Speculative decoding improves latency by using a small, fast 'draft' model to propose multiple tokens in parallel, then verifying them with the large 'target' model. For example, a 1B parameter draft model generates 5 candidate tokens in 50ms. The target model (GPT-4 scale) then processes all 5 tokens in parallel in a single forward pass (200ms) and checks if they match what it would have generated. Accepted tokens are kept, and generation continues from the first rejected token. This approach provides 2-3x speedup when the draft model's predictions align well with the target model. OpenAI trains specialized draft models that mimic the target model's behavior on specific domains (code, chat, creative writing) to maximize acceptance rate. Speculative decoding is especially effective for short completions (10-50 tokens) where setup overhead is amortized quickly, improving interactive chat latency significantly.

sections.title: Agent Orchestration Framework
sections.content: Meta's AI agents (powering features like Meta AI in WhatsApp/Instagram) use an orchestration framework that manages multi-turn conversations, tool use, and memory. The architecture follows a modular design with components: orchestrator (coordinates agent execution), tool registry (available tools and their schemas), memory manager (conversation history and context), and LLM engine (Llama models). When a user sends a message, the orchestrator builds a prompt including conversation history, available tools, and system instructions. The LLM generates a response, potentially including tool calls formatted as JSON. If tool calls are present, the orchestrator executes them (e.g., web search, calculator, image generation), injects results into the prompt, and calls the LLM again to generate the final response. This cycle continues until the LLM returns a final answer without tool calls. The framework supports parallel tool execution when multiple independent tools are needed, reducing latency. Tool timeout handling ensures the agent remains responsive even if external APIs are slow.

sections.title: Llama Tool Use and Function Calling
sections.content: Meta fine-tuned Llama models specifically for tool use, training them to generate structured function calls when appropriate. The training dataset includes examples where the model should use tools (e.g., 'What's the weather in Tokyo?' → web_search('Tokyo weather')) and examples where tools aren't needed (e.g., 'What is 2+2?' → direct answer without calculator tool). Function calling output follows a strict JSON schema: {tool: 'web_search', parameters: {query: 'Tokyo weather'}}. The model is trained to always use tools when real-time or verifiable information is required, reducing hallucinations. Meta's tool use training balances precision (call tools when needed) and recall (don't overuse tools for simple questions). The model achieves 92% precision and 88% recall on tool use benchmarks. Fine-tuning used reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) where human raters judged whether tool use was appropriate, creating a reward signal that guides the model toward better tool selection.

sections.title: Conversation Memory and Context Management
sections.content: Meta AI agents maintain conversation memory across sessions to provide personalized, contextually aware responses. Memory is stored in three tiers: short-term (current conversation, stored in Redis with 1-hour TTL), medium-term (recent conversations, stored in Cassandra with 30-day TTL), and long-term (user preferences and facts, stored in MySQL indefinitely). When a user sends a message, the memory manager retrieves relevant context from all tiers using a hybrid approach: short-term memory is fully included (the entire current conversation), medium-term memory is filtered by recency and relevance (last 5 conversations or semantically similar past conversations), and long-term memory is queried using embeddings (user preferences related to the current topic). The combined context is summarized if it exceeds the model's context window (8K tokens for Llama 2, 32K for Llama 3) using an extractive summarization model. This tiered memory approach balances context richness with computational cost.

sections.title: Safety and Moderation Pipeline
sections.content: AI agents accessible to billions of users require robust safety mechanisms to prevent harmful outputs. Meta implements a multi-layered safety pipeline: input filtering (block malicious prompts using keyword and ML-based classifiers), inference-time guardrails (constrain model outputs using controlled generation), and output filtering (detect and block harmful generated content). Input filtering uses a gradient boosted tree model trained on adversarial prompt datasets, catching jailbreak attempts with 95% precision. Inference-time guardrails use custom Llama fine-tuning with safety instructions and Constitutional AI principles, training the model to refuse harmful requests while remaining helpful. Output filtering runs generated text through toxicity classifiers before showing to users. Additionally, the agent framework has hard limits: conversation length capped at 20 turns (to prevent circular reasoning), generation length capped at 500 tokens, and tool execution timeout at 5 seconds. These safety layers have reduced policy-violating outputs to under 0.01% while maintaining agent usefulness.

sections.title: Delta Lake for ACID Transactions
sections.content: Databricks built Delta Lake, an open-source storage layer that brings ACID transaction guarantees to data lakes. Traditional data lakes (files in S3/ADLS) lack transactional consistency—concurrent writers can corrupt data, and readers might see partial writes. Delta Lake solves this using a transaction log (similar to database WAL) implemented as JSON files in S3. Each transaction appends a new commit file to the _delta_log directory with metadata about added/removed files and transaction information. Readers first read the transaction log to determine which data files are valid for their read timestamp, ensuring consistent snapshot isolation. The transaction log uses optimistic concurrency control—writers read the latest version, apply changes locally, then attempt to commit by writing a new transaction log entry. If another writer committed in the meantime, the transaction retries. This approach provides serializability without requiring a central coordinator. Delta Lake also implements Z-ordering (multi-dimensional clustering) and file compaction to optimize query performance. The architecture enables data lakes to support both batch analytics and streaming workloads with consistency guarantees previously only available in data warehouses.

sections.title: Unity Catalog for Data Governance
sections.content: Unity Catalog is Databricks' unified governance layer providing fine-grained access control, data lineage, and auditing across data lakes.
