The catalog implements a three-level namespace: catalogs (highest level, typically one per organization), schemas (logical grouping of tables), and tables/views. Access control uses role-based permissions (RBAC) with privileges like SELECT, MODIFY, CREATE defined at each level and inherited hierarchically. Unity Catalog integrates with identity providers (Azure AD, Okta) for authentication and supports both user and service principal access. Data lineage automatically tracks table dependencies—when a table is created via a query joining other tables, Unity Catalog records the lineage graph. This enables impact analysis (what downstream tables will break if I delete this table?) and compliance reporting. Column-level access control allows masking sensitive data—for example, PII columns can be restricted to specific roles while other columns remain accessible. The catalog metadata is stored in a distributed key-value store (likely DynamoDB or Cosmos DB) with caching for fast access. Unity Catalog unified previously fragmented governance solutions across AWS, Azure, and GCP, providing consistent security regardless of cloud provider.

sections.title: Photon Vectorized Query Engine
sections.content: Photon is Databricks' C++ vectorized query engine designed to replace Spark's JVM-based execution for high-performance queries. Traditional Spark processes data row-by-row with significant per-row overhead from JVM object allocation and virtual method calls. Photon uses columnar execution processing batches of thousands of rows at once, enabling CPU vectorization (SIMD instructions) that process multiple values per instruction. For example, an 'add' operation on two columns can add 8 integers simultaneously using AVX2 instructions. Photon compiles query plans to optimized machine code using LLVM, eliminating interpretation overhead. The engine uses adaptive execution analyzing runtime statistics to optimize join strategies and shuffle partition counts mid-query. Photon achieves 2-10x speedup over Spark SQL for typical queries, with largest gains on selective filters and aggregations. The architecture is compatible with Spark APIs—users write standard Spark SQL or DataFrame code, and Databricks runtime automatically uses Photon when beneficial. Photon adoption has been gradual with staged rollout to ensure compatibility. The engine is proprietary but integrates with open-source Delta Lake and Spark.

sections.title: Serverless Compute for Instant Clusters
sections.content: Databricks Serverless eliminates cluster management by providing instant compute that auto-scales transparently. Traditional Databricks workflows require users to create clusters (specifying instance types and count), wait for provisioning (5-10 minutes), then run jobs. Serverless pre-provisions warm pools of compute instances in Databricks' AWS/Azure accounts, shared across customers with security isolation via containers. When a user runs a query, it's routed to available capacity in milliseconds. The system uses bin-packing algorithms to efficiently allocate resources—small queries share large instances, while big queries get dedicated instances. Isolation uses Kubernetes pods with strict cgroups limiting CPU/memory per query. Billing is per-DBU (Databricks Unit) per second with 1-minute minimum, making short queries cost-effective. Serverless compute automatically scales up when queries are queued and scales down when idle, optimizing cost. The warm pool management is complex—Databricks predicts demand patterns and pre-warms capacity in each region to minimize cold starts. Serverless has become the default for Databricks SQL and notebooks, significantly lowering the barrier to adoption by eliminating infrastructure decisions.

sections.title: Block-Level Chunking Algorithm
sections.content: Dropbox's sync engine uses block-level deduplication and delta sync to minimize bandwidth. When a file is added, the sync client chunks it into 4MB blocks using rolling hash (Rabin fingerprinting). Each block is hashed using SHA-256 to generate a unique identifier. The client queries Dropbox servers to check which blocks already exist (uploaded by this user or others). Only new blocks are uploaded, and the file metadata references the block hashes. This approach provides massive savings—if you add a 100MB file that your colleague already uploaded, only metadata is transmitted (~1KB instead of 100MB). When modifying a file, the chunking algorithm identifies which blocks changed. For a 1GB video file where you edit 10 seconds (approximately 10MB), only the affected blocks (~3 blocks, 12MB) are uploaded. The rolling hash ensures chunk boundaries are content-based rather than fixed offsets, maximizing deduplication even when insertions/deletions shift file contents. This algorithm requires careful tuning—smaller chunks increase deduplication but create overhead from more metadata, while larger chunks reduce deduplication benefits.

sections.title: Conflict Detection and Resolution
sections.content: Dropbox handles concurrent edits through conflict detection and resolution. Each file has a version number (monotonically increasing). When a client modifies a file, it reads the current version number, makes local changes, then attempts to upload with a version constraint (If-Match: version=N). If another client uploaded a new version in the meantime, the conditional upload fails. The client then has a conflict: local version based on version N, but server is now at version N+1. Dropbox resolves this by creating a conflicted copy: the original file is set to the server version, and the local changes are saved as 'filename (conflicted copy 2025-01-15).txt'. This preserves both versions without data loss. The user can manually merge if needed. For real-time collaborative editing (Dropbox Paper), the system uses operational transformation—edits are represented as operations (insert character at position X), and a conflict resolution algorithm merges concurrent operations deterministically. This allows multiple users to edit simultaneously without creating conflicted copies. File-level sync uses the simpler conflict detection approach while document-level collaboration uses operational transformation.

sections.title: Real-Time Sync Notification System
sections.content: Dropbox clients must be notified in real-time when files change on the server to pull updates. The original implementation used polling (check for updates every 60 seconds), wasting bandwidth and battery on mobile devices. Modern Dropbox uses a push notification system built on long-polling and WebSockets. When a client starts, it opens a long-lived HTTP connection to the notification server and subscribes to its namespace (the user's account). When files change on the server (upload from another device), the notification system publishes a message to the user's notification channel. All connected clients receive the notification within 1 second, triggering immediate sync. The notification payload is minimal—it contains a namespace ID and a revision number, not the actual file content. Clients then query the metadata API to fetch details of changed files. The notification infrastructure uses a pub-sub system built on AWS services: API Gateway WebSocket for maintaining client connections, SNS/SQS for message routing, and Lambda for processing. This architecture scales to millions of simultaneous connections with minimal cost compared to polling. Mobile apps use Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) for push notifications when the app is backgrounded, triggering background sync.

sections.title: Magic Pocket Storage Backend
sections.content: Dropbox built Magic Pocket, a custom distributed storage system, to reduce dependence on AWS S3 and optimize for their workload. Magic Pocket is deployed across Dropbox's own data centers with petabytes of storage. The architecture uses erasure coding (Reed-Solomon) for durability—each block is encoded into N fragments with M parity fragments, allowing reconstruction if any M fragments are lost. Dropbox uses 14 data fragments + 6 parity fragments, providing 99.999999999% durability while using only 1.4x storage overhead (compared to 3x for triple replication). Blocks are distributed across racks and data centers to tolerate failures. Dropbox uses SMR (Shingled Magnetic Recording) hard drives, optimized for write-once workloads, achieving 40% higher density than conventional drives. Metadata (which blocks belong to which files) is stored in a distributed database separate from block storage. This separation allows metadata queries without touching block storage, improving performance for operations like listing folder contents. Magic Pocket significantly reduced Dropbox's infrastructure costs while giving them full control over storage, enabling optimizations tailored to their sync workload patterns.
